WHAT WAS WRONG (reproduced first, on the real registerType + recordEntry path, before any code changed): the generated per-type view claims a flat column namespace. SQLite does NOT error on a duplicate column name in a CREATE VIEW; it keeps the first and renames the loser to <name>:1. With envelope columns projected first, a property named 'source' yielded columns ["source","source:1","source_state"], and the exact query ARCHITECTURE.md prescribes returned {"source":"self","id":"e1"} -- the ENVELOPE value under the property's name, with no error. A wrong answer that looks right, which is the class this product exists to prevent.

THE FIX. @ascend/core owns the vocabulary: ENVELOPE_PROPERTY_NAMES (the 16 columns a view projects, in projection order), STATE_COLUMN_SUFFIX, reservedPropertyName(raw), and a NEW 'errors' bucket on Canonicalized<T> beside renames/warnings. Errors are a different KIND, not a higher severity: a warning is a legal spec someone probably did not mean; an error is one no canonicalization can rescue. registerType throws ReservedPropertyNameError before writing anything; refreshTypeViews->assertProjectable refuses before any DDL, as the second line for a version row that reached the store without the registry. packages/store/src/sql.ts projects FROM core's list, so the reserved set and the projected set cannot drift apart.

TWO SHAPE DECISIONS WORTH THE RECORD. (1) The _state suffix rule is UNCONDITIONAL even though a collision needs two properties, because versions arrive one at a time: admitting error_state in v1 would leave a registered family that v2 could never extend with 'error'. (2) reservedPropertyName canonicalizes its own input, so no spelling (Source, gitSHA, Recorded At) gets around the rule. Deliberately NOT reserved, measured rather than assumed: ascend_version and schema_version are entries columns the view does not project, so they stay legal; and '_state' canonicalizes to 'state', which nothing claims -- the real case is 'error_state', never the literal '_state'.

WHAT WAS WRONG (reproduced first on the real binary, before any code changed): `asc types define`
with an empty property name exited 0 with only a warning, and the store was then permanently unable
to record ANY type -- `bad JSON path: '$.'`, exit 1 -- while `types list` and `types brief` still
exited 0, so it looked healthy. The index that `views.ts` builds is on `entries`, not on one type, so
SQLite evaluated the empty JSON path for every INSERT. No repair path: entries are immutable, types
cannot be deleted, no command drops an index.

THE FIX, two branches in `spec.ts`. The property case moved from `warnings` to `errors` (the sibling
reserved-name case was already an error, for a strictly smaller reason -- that split was the bug).
The TYPE name case had NO check at all and reached the store's `name <> ''` CHECK, measured as
`Error: CHECK constraint failed: name <> ''` -- naming neither canonicalization, the name, nor the
fix -- so it is now refused in the same place. Nothing new is refused beyond names that cannot work.

THE ERROR CLASS WAS RENAMED, and it is not cosmetic: `ReservedPropertyNameError` was accurate while a
reserved collision was the only way to reach it, and its message said "N property name(s) in '<type>'

Two corrections to the report's framing, both measured:

1. The defect is NESTED, not top level. z.record already refuses Date/Map/Set at the top level -- zod's own type detection calls them date/map/set. It is z.unknown() as an array element or record value that waves anything through. The first probe version offered a Date directly, printed ok:false, and "failed to reproduce" a bug that was there all along -- which is how a real defect gets recorded as already fixed. That is why the report's evidence line reads {"v":[{}]}.

2. The check reads the RAW offered value, not parsed.data. z.record ACCEPTS a RegExp (zod calls it a plain object), walks its zero own enumerable keys, and returns a fresh {} -- so downstream of zod the RegExp is unobservable. Found by a test that failed after the fix looked complete.

Swept the class: a symbol-keyed or non-enumerable member is dropped by Object.entries and by zod's record walk alike, so a member the recorder attached was silently absent for the same reason. Both refused now.

canonicalJson is deliberately UNCHANGED -- it drops undefined inside an object and typeHash depends on that. An entry property with the same drop would resolve measured with no key in the row, so the validator refuses it instead. Two contracts, difference decided in a comment.

FIXED. One commit. Write-side halves in both writers plus the CLI's mirror path; the data half is answered by measurement rather than by a repair pass, and one stated premise of this bead is REFUTED by that measurement.

WHAT WAS BUILT. registry.ts gains `canonicalProseKeys(typeName, spec, prose)`, called from `toStorage` (before the whole-registration transaction, so a refusal writes nothing and mints no version) and from `updateTypeProse`. It folds each key with `canonicalName`, refuses a key that names no declared property with `UnusableProseError` listing the declared names, and refuses two declarations that fold to one property rather than silently resolving them. `updateTypeProse` deliberately does NOT re-key `existing.prose` -- renaming a caller's unrelated stored prose is a different decision from refusing the key they just sent. The CLI half is `register-document.ts:136`: the mirror path compared the document's raw key against the store's folded map, so an idempotent `asc types define` reported `prose-updated` on the second run of the same file. Measured by removing the fold and watching the test fail with `expected 'prose-updated' to be 'unchanged'`.

THE STATED PREMISE, REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT. This bead's note argues a repair pass is expensive because "normalizing a key changes type_hash, so re-registering that spec would mint a new version rather than matching the old one," citing F7's trimming rejection as the same class. Measured on a copy of the one real defective store: rewriting its prose through `updateTypeProse` leaves `type_hash` byte-identical (`d9cf4752366c` before and after) and `spec_json` untouched. Prose is outside the hash by construction -- `definitionShape` drops it -- which is the same property the report's prose-is-not-identity tests rest on. The note conflated a prose KEY with a spec PROPERTY NAME; only the latter is inside the hash. The type_hash objection to a repair does not exist.

WHAT DOES BLOCK A FULL REWRITE, also measured, and NOT the reason stated. `updateTypeProse` cannot REMOVE a stale key: repairing the defective row through the store's own writer produced `{"reviewKind":"how the review ended","review_kind":"how the review ended"}` -- the merge is `{...existing.prose, ...canonical}` with `existing.prose` never re-keyed, so the old key lingers. The prose becomes VISIBLE and the stale key remains. No API deletes a prose key, and building one would be a mechanism with no evidence behind it.

DATA HALF, CLOSED WITH NUMBERS. Read-only scan of every store on this machine: 386 found, 381 opened, 5 unreadable, 1,063 type rows. Keys under a non-canonical spelling: 1 -- `/var/folders/41/.../asc-v-Z2KKQb/ascend.db`, `review_completed` v1, stored `reviewKind` (canonical `review_kind`). Keys naming no property of their own version: 0. So the defect exists once, and the new refusal refuses nothing that exists -- no real registry round trip breaks. That one row was driven end to end through the real CLI: `asc types export | asc types import -` into a fresh project turns `prose_json` into `{"review_kind":"how the review ended"}`, and `asc types show` goes from reporting that property's description as `null` to reporting the prose. So the repair path that works is the ROUND TRIP, already shipped; no migration and no repair pass. Residual: one stale key on one row of 1,063, in a scratch store this audit itself created. Not worth a prose-removal API.
